smt-2014-calculus-02.title: Tangent line
smt-2014-calculus-02.body:
The tangent at $x=a$ has slope $2a$: $y-(a^2+1)=2a(x-a)$. Passing through $(0,0)$ requires $-(a^2+1)=-2a^2$, so $a^2=1$ and $a=1$ (positive).

**Answer: 1**

smt-2014-calculus-03.title: Maximise expected log
smt-2014-calculus-03.body:
After heads Moor has $1000(1+5k)$ dollars, after tails $1000(1-k)$. Expected happiness $H(k)=\frac12\ln(1000(1+5k))+\frac12\ln(1000(1-k))$, i.e. up to constants $\ln\big((1+5k)(1-k)\big)$. The product $(1+5k)(1-k)=1+4k-5k^2$ is a downward parabola maximised at $k=\frac{4}{10}=\frac25$, which is in $[0,1]$, and $\ln$ is increasing.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

smt-2014-calculus-03.title: Derivative
smt-2014-calculus-03.body:
$H'(k)=\frac12\left(\frac5{1+5k}-\frac1{1-k}\right)$, which is positive for $k<\frac25$ and negative for $\frac25<k<1$ (it vanishes when $5(1-k)=1+5k$). So $H$ increases then decreases on $[0,1)$, and the maximum is at $k=\frac25$; at $k=1$ the tails outcome has zero money and the happiness is $-\infty$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

smt-2014-calculus-04.title: Quadrant integral
smt-2014-calculus-04.body:
The curve is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$ and $y\mapsto-y$ (note $x^{2/5}=(x^{1/5})^2$ is defined and even). In the first quadrant, $y=1-x^{2/5}$ for $0\le x\le1$, so the area there is $\int_0^1(1-x^{2/5})\,dx=1-\frac57=\frac27$. The total area is $4\cdot\frac27=\frac87$.

**Answer: $\frac87$**

smt-2014-calculus-05.title: Antiderivative
smt-2014-calculus-05.body:
Combine over a common denominator: $\sqrt{\frac{4-x}x}-\sqrt{\frac x{4-x}}=\frac{(4-x)-x}{\sqrt{x(4-x)}}=\frac{4-2x}{\sqrt{4x-x^2}}$. With $u=4x-x^2$, $du=(4-2x)dx$, the integral becomes $\int_0^4u^{-1/2}\,du=2\sqrt u\Big|_0^4=4$.

**Answer: 4**

smt-2014-calculus-05.title: Trig substitution
smt-2014-calculus-05.body:
Let $x=4\sin^2\theta$, $0\le\theta\le\frac\pi4$. Then $\sqrt{\frac{4-x}x}=\cot\theta$, $dx=8\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$, and the integral is $8\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cot\theta-\tan\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=8\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos2\theta\,d\theta=4$.

**Answer: 4**

smt-2014-calculus-06.title: L'Hôpital
smt-2014-calculus-06.body:
Put $t=\frac1x\to0^+$: the expression is $\frac{t-\ln(1+t)}{t^2}$. Applying L'Hôpital: $\frac{1-\frac1{1+t}}{2t}=\frac{t/(1+t)}{2t}=\frac1{2(1+t)}\to\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

smt-2014-calculus-07.title: Fixed points
smt-2014-calculus-07.body:
If $a_n\to L$ then $x^L=L$, i.e. $x=L^{1/L}$. The function $L\mapsto L^{1/L}=e^{(\ln L)/L}$ has derivative $L^{1/L}\cdot\frac{1-\ln L}{L^2}$, so it increases for $L<e$, decreases for $L>e$, and has maximum $e^{1/e}$ at $L=e$. Hence a convergent sequence forces $x\le e^{1/e}$.

Conversely, for $x=e^{1/e}$ the sequence is increasing and bounded by $e$ (if $a_n<e$ then $a_{n+1}=x^{a_n}<x^e=e$), so it converges (to $e$). For $x>e^{1/e}$ no fixed point exists, i.e. $x^t>t$ for all $t$, so $a_n$ is strictly increasing and cannot converge. The largest $x$ is $e^{1/e}$.

**Answer: $e^{1/e}$**

smt-2014-calculus-08.title: Symmetry trick
smt-2014-calculus-08.body:
Let $I$ be the integral. Substituting $x\to-x$ gives $I=\int_{-2}^2\frac{(1+x^2)2^x}{2^x+1}\,dx$. Adding the two forms: $2I=\int_{-2}^2(1+x^2)\frac{1+2^x}{1+2^x}dx=\int_{-2}^2(1+x^2)\,dx=4+\frac{16}3=\frac{28}3$. So $I=\frac{14}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}3$**

smt-2014-calculus-09.title: Area under an inverse function
smt-2014-calculus-09.body:
$f$ is the inverse of $g(y)=ye^y$ on $y\ge0$, with $f(0)=0$ and $f(e)=1$ (since $g(1)=e$). The area under $f$ from $0$ to $e$ equals the area of the rectangle $[0,e]\times[0,1]$ minus the area under $g$ from $0$ to $1$: $\int_0^ef=e-\int_0^1ye^y\,dy$. By parts, $\int_0^1ye^y\,dy=[ye^y]_0^1-\int_0^1e^y\,dy=e-(e-1)=1$. So the integral is $e-1$.

**Answer: $e-1$**

smt-2014-calculus-09.title: Substitution
smt-2014-calculus-09.body:
With $u=f(x)$, $x=ue^u$, $dx=(1+u)e^u\,du$, and the limits $x=0,e$ correspond to $u=0,1$: $\int_0^ef(x)\,dx=\int_0^1u(1+u)e^u\,du=\left[e^u(u^2-u+1)\right]_0^1=e-1$.

**Answer: $e-1$**

smt-2014-calculus-10.title: Dilogarithm reflection
smt-2014-calculus-10.body:
Let $L(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n^2}$ for $|x|\le1$; we want $L(\frac12)$. Differentiating, $xL'(x)=\sum x^n/n$, so $L'(x)=-\frac{\ln(1-x)}x$.

Consider $h(x)=L(x)+L(1-x)+\ln x\ln(1-x)$ on $(0,1)$. Then $h'(x)=-\frac{\ln(1-x)}x+\frac{\ln x}{1-x}+\frac{\ln(1-x)}x-\frac{\ln x}{1-x}=0$, so $h$ is constant. As $x\to0^+$: $L(x)\to0$, $L(1-x)\to L(1)=\frac{\pi^2}6$, and $\ln x\ln(1-x)\sim-x\ln x\to0$. So $h\equiv\frac{\pi^2}6$. At $x=\frac12$: $2L(\frac12)+\ln^22=\frac{\pi^2}6$, so
$$L\left(\tfrac12\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{\ln^22}2.$$

**Answer: $\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{\ln^22}2$**
